latestRelease.title: v1.64.0/v0.158.0
latestRelease.notes:
### Images and binaries here: https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector-releases/releases/tag/v0.158.0

## End User Changelog

### 🚀 New components 🚀

- `processor/queuebatch`: New `queuebatchprocessor` to replace the legacy `batchprocessor`. (#15047, #13582, #12022, #11308, #8272, #6046)
  New implementation is based exporterhelper, uses same configuration as `sending_queue`.

### 💡 Enhancements 💡

- `cmd/mdatagen`: Add first-class extended type aliases (int64, duration, opaque_string, id, opaque_map, etc.) to config schemas in metadata.yaml (#15513)
  Authors can now write `type: int64`, `type: duration`, `type: opaque_string`, `type: id`, or
  `type: opaque_map` directly as a property type in the `config:` section of `metadata.yaml`.
  Each alias expands to the correct JSON Schema representation and Go type automatically.
  Existing uses of standard JSON Schema types, `format:`, and `x-customType:` remain supported
  without migration.
  
- `extension/memory_limiter`: Promote the memory limiter extension to beta stability. (#14533)

### 🧰 Bug fixes 🧰

- `cmd/mdatagen`: Removes the extra line in the documentation.md around description (#15664)
- `cmd/mdatagen`: Auto-enable v1 metrics when legacy metric is enabled and v1 feature gate is on (#15650)
  When the v1 feature gate is enabled and a legacy metric is enabled, the corresponding
  v1 metric is now programmatically enabled so users don't need to add the v1 metric
  to their config.
  
- `cmd/mdatagen`: Fix incorrect collision warning for versioned metrics with different emitted names (#15648)
  Same name collision detection (type/attribute checks) was being used for versioned metrics
  with different names. This caused the legacy metric to be disabled which was incorrect and also
  a warning msg was being incorrectly logged that stated the metrics had the same name when in
  fact they had different names.
  
- `cmd/mdatagen`: Versioned metrics don't handle renamed attributes with same type (#15595)
  Versioned metrics need to support emitting legacy and latest attributes when the metric name is the same but the
  attributes names differ. This was not working when the attributes name changed but the type remained the same.
  Here we add support to versioned metrics with renamed attributes where those attributes have the same type.
  
- `exporter/debug`: Fix profile sample attribute formatting for non-string values (#15647)
  Previously, non-string values produced malformed output such as `%!s(int64=42)`.
  Profile sample attributes now use the debug exporter's typed attribute format, such as `Int(42)`.
  This will also change strings from `hello-world` to `Str(hello-world)`.
  
- `pkg/config/configtls`: Fix goroutine and file descriptor leak when `client_ca_file_reload` is enabled (#9221)
  Every call to `ServerConfig.LoadTLSConfig` with `client_ca_file_reload` enabled started a
  file watcher goroutine that could never be stopped, since the reloader was not reachable
  from the returned `*tls.Config`. The client CA file is now checked for changes while TLS
  handshakes are served, at most once per second, matching how `reload_interval` already
  reloads the server certificate. No background goroutine is started, so nothing is left
  behind when a server is torn down and recreated.

## API Changelog

### 🛑 Breaking changes 🛑

- `pkg/xconfmap`: Remove `Validator` and `Validate` (#15613)
  Use the equivalent symbols in `confmap` instead.

### 💡 Enhancements 💡

- `cmd/mdatagen`: Add first-class extended type aliases (int64, duration, opaque_string, id, opaque_map, etc.) to config schemas in metadata.yaml (#15513)
  Authors can now write `type: int64`, `type: duration`, `type: opaque_string`, `type: id`, or
  `type: opaque_map` directly as a property type in the `config:` section of `metadata.yaml`.
  Each alias expands to the correct JSON Schema representation and Go type automatically.
  Existing uses of standard JSON Schema types, `format:`, and `x-customType:` remain supported
  without migration.
  
- `pkg/config/configgrpc`: Mark configgrpc as stable (#9477)

signals.title: [pdata/pprofile] Speed up dictionary merging with an indexed dedup
signals.text: #### Description Hi! In #15084 the cost of merging the profiles dictionary came up (and @dmathieu mentioned [improvement points would be welcome](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/issues/15084#issuecomment-4222053064)), so I took a look at the merge path. The cost is in `Profiles.MergeTo` → `switchDictionary`: every `Set*` does a linear `.Equal` scan of the destination table, once per source entry, which makes a merge quadratic in dictionary size. This PR adds an internal per-merge index (`mergeIndex`) — one lookup structure per table, seeded once from the destination — to replace those scans. The string table uses a `map[string]int32`; the other tables use a hash bucket where the existing `.Equal` is still the arbiter (the hash only narrows candidates), so dedup semantics are unchanged. The public `Set*` API is untouched — only the unexported `switchDictionary` methods change. Output is byte-identical to before (lowest-index-wins preserved), covered by a differential test, a forced hash-collision test, and an end-to-end marshal→merge→unmarshal round-trip. Attribute entries are hashed by the content of their value, not just its type, so a table dominated by one hot key (`thread.name`, `k8s.pod.name`) still spreads across buckets. The value hash has to agree with `pcommon.Value.Equal` or equal values would land in different buckets and append a duplicate where the linear scan deduped: `-0.0` is normalized to `+0.0` (`Equal` compares doubles with `==`), and maps are combined order-independently (`Map.Equal` matches by key, and Go's map iteration order is randomized). **Benchmarks.** `BenchmarkDictionaryMerge` merges a batch of K profiles into one destination. I don't know the real-world distribution of how much profiles in a batch share dictionary symbols, so I swept it: `overlap` is the fraction of a profile's dictionary already present in the destination (0% = fully disjoint, the worst case; 100% = identical profiles). benchstat, n=10, `main` → this PR (AMD Ryzen 7 255, linux/amd64), 20-profile batch: | case | main | this PR | Δ time | |---|---|---|---| | overlap=0% (disjoint) | 65.69 s | 124.0 ms | −99.81% | | overlap=50% | 3.405 s | 78.5 ms | −97.69% | | overlap=90% | 2.738 s | 48.7 ms | −98.22% | | overlap=99% | 3.140 s | 42.0 ms | −98.66% | | batch=5 | 672.9 ms | 11.7 ms | −98.26% | | batch=20 | 2.741 s | 49.3 ms | −98.20% | | batch=50 | 7.100 s | 137.0 ms | −98.07% | | size=0.5x | 709.6 ms | 25.0 ms | −96.48% | | size=1x | 2.741 s | 50.2 ms | −98.17% | | size=2x | 11.12 s | 96.5 ms | −99.13% | | **geomean** | **3.746 s** | **53.5 ms** | **−98.57%** | `BenchmarkDictionaryMergeHotKey` isolates the attribute table under a single hot key carrying many distinct values — the shape that stays quadratic if attribute values are hashed by type rather than content. 10-profile batch: | case | main | this PR | Δ time | |---|---|---|---| | attrs=500 | 8.99 ms | 632 µs | −92.97% | | attrs=2000 | 139.2 ms | 4.18 ms | −97.00% | | attrs=8000 | 2.344 s | 17.0 ms | −99.27% | | **geomean** | **143.1 ms** | **3.56 ms** | **−97.52%** | All differences p=0.000 at n=10. Scaling with dictionary size goes from quadratic to ~linear. Reproduce: `go test ./pdata/pprofile/ -bench BenchmarkDictionaryMerge -benchmem` on this branch vs `main`. Tradeoff: the index trades transient memory for CPU, and the trade is not small in absolute terms. Geomean `B/op` goes up +948% on the sweep (+441% allocs/op) and +947% on the hot-key benchmark (+384%). Since a percentage hides the number worth budgeting for, the peaks: 12.66 MiB → 100.9 MiB per merge at `overlap=0%`, and 3.48 MiB → 68.8 MiB at `batch=50`. The index is rebuilt per `MergeTo`, so it is short-lived garbage freed when the merge returns — but it is a real peak, not an average. If the extra allocation or GC pressure is a concern, the per-merge rebuild can be removed entirely with a destination-resident index or a once-per-flush batch-merge entry point — I kept this PR to the merge path only to stay tightly scoped, and can follow up with that if you'd prefer. #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15544. Related to #15084 (the perf half; the data-corruption half was fixed in #15134). #### Testing New differential + hash-collision tests (`dictionary_merge_index_test.go`) covering every table, including a same-key/distinct-value case for attributes with a bucket-spread assertion; tests that the value hash agrees with `Equal` on `-0.0` and on map ordering; a zero-allocation guard on the value hash; table-overflow guard coverage; and an end-to-end round-trip (`profiles_merge_test.go`). Each new guard was verified to fail without the corresponding fix. `go test ./pdata/pprofile/...` (including `-race`) and `go vet ./pdata/pprofile/` pass, as do the `pdata`, root, `exporter/exporterhelper` and `scraper/scraperhelper` module suites. #### Documentation Changelog entry under `.chloggen/`. #### Authorship - [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.

[#​3973](https://redirect.github.com/github/codeql-action/pull/3973) </details> <details> <summary>lycheeverse/lychee-action (lycheeverse/lychee-action)</summary> ### [`v2.9.0`](https://redirect.github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/releases/tag/v2.9.0) [Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/compare/v2.8.0...v2.9.0) #### Summary This release updates the default lychee version from `v0.23.0` to `v0.24.2`. The main reason for this release is compatibility with the new lychee `0.24.x` release artifacts. Starting with lychee `v0.24.0`, the archive layout changed, and the `lychee` binary may now be packaged inside a subdirectory. `lychee-action` now detects that layout automatically, so users can upgrade without changing their workflows. If you use: ```yaml uses: lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2 ``` you will get the new version once the floating `v2` tag has been updated. If you pin exact versions, update to: ```yaml uses: lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2.9.0 ``` #### What’s new from lychee `v0.24.x` ##### Better diagnostics lychee now reports line and column numbers for detected links. This makes broken link reports easier to act on, especially in larger documentation sites or generated reports. ##### Text fragment checking lychee can now check URL text fragments, such as links containing `#:~:text=...`. This helps catch links that point to a valid page but no longer points to the intended highlighted text. ##### Sitemap support lychee can now read `sitemap.xml` inputs. This is useful for checking published websites or generated documentation sites where the sitemap is the easiest source of URLs to validate. ##### JUnit output lychee now supports JUnit output. This makes it easier to integrate link checking results with CI systems and test reporting tools that understand JUnit XML. ##### Redirect and remap visibility lychee can now show redirects and remaps more clearly. This helps explain why a URL was checked as a different final URL and makes debugging link-checking behavior easier. ##### Multiple config files lychee now supports multiple configuration files and expanded config handling. This is useful for repositories that split documentation, website, or package-specific link-checking settings. ##### Timeout handling lychee can now accept timeouts explicitly. This gives users more control over how strict their link checks should be for flaky or slow endpoints. #### Fixes and reliability improvements ##### Fixed lychee `0.24.x` archive compatibility `lychee-action` now handles the new lychee release archive layout by detecting whether the `lychee` binary is inside a subdirectory. This fixes compatibility with lychee `0.24.x`. ##### More stable installation path The action now installs lychee into `$RUNNER_TEMP/lychee/bin` instead of `$HOME`. This avoids failures on runners where `$HOME` differs between composite action steps. In those environments, the action could add one directory to `PATH` but install the binary somewhere else, causing `lychee: command not found`. ##### Safer automatic lychee version updates The workflow that checks for new lychee releases now guards against `null` release versions before creating update PRs. This prevents invalid automated PRs such as “Update lycheeVersion to null”. ##### Dependency updates - Updated `actions/checkout` from `v6` to `v7` - Updated `actions/cache` from `v5` to `v6` #### Upstream lychee changelog For the full lychee changelog, see: - <https://github.com/lycheeverse/lychee/releases/tag/lychee-v0.24.0> - <https://github.com/lycheeverse/lychee/releases/tag/lychee-v0.24.1> - <https://github.com/lycheeverse/lychee/releases/tag/lychee-v0.24.2> #### What’s Changed - bump default to 0.24.1 and auto-detect lychee bin in subfolder by [@​kaitlyndotmoe](https://redirect.github.com/kaitlyndotmoe) in [#​330](https://redirect.github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/pull/330) - fixes [#​322](https://redirect.github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/issues/322) check for null by [@​bgermann](https://redirect.github.com/bgermann) in [#​336](https://redirect.github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/pull/336) - Install into `$RUNNER_TEMP` instead of `$HOME` by [@​mre](https://redirect.github.com/mre) in [#​338](https://redirect.github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/pull/338) - Bump actions/checkout from 6 to 7 by [@​dependabot](https://redirect.github.com/dependabot) in [#​339](https://redirect.github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/pull/339) - Bump actions/cache from 5 to 6 by [@​dependabot](https://redirect.github.com/dependabot) in [#​340](https://redirect.github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/pull/340) **Full Changelog**: <https://github.com/lycheeverse/lychee-action/compare/v2.8.0...v2.9.0> </details> <details> <summary>ossf/scorecard-action (ossf/scorecard-action)</summary> ### [`v2.4.4`](https://redirect.github.com/ossf/scorecard-action/releases/tag/v2.4.4) [Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/ossf/scorecard-action/compare/v2.4.3...v2.4.4) #### What's Changed This update bumps the Scorecard version to the v5.5.0 release. signals.title: Add recursion depth limit to JSON unmarshalling
signals.text: #### Description The proto unmarshal path bounds recursion depth to guard against stack exhaustion from deeply nested payloads, but the JSON path had no equivalent limit. An `AnyValue` whose value is an `arrayValue`/`kvlistValue` of `AnyValue`s, nested deeply enough, recurses through the generated `UnmarshalJSON` methods until the goroutine stack overflows — a fatal, unrecoverable crash (`recover()` cannot catch it), not just a failed request. It's reachable through the public `JSONUnmarshaler` from any component that decodes untrusted OTLP/JSON without a request-size cap. This tracks nesting depth on the JSON `Iterator` (`EnterRecursive`/`ExitRecursive`, with a limit of 100) and injects the guard at the top of every generated `UnmarshalJSON` via the pdatagen template, so over-limit nesting returns an error instead of overflowing the stack. This mirrors the proto side (#15597). The limit sits well beyond any realistic telemetry nesting — the effective budget is ~47 nested `arrayValue`/`kvlistValue` levels, matching the proto path — so well-formed payloads are unaffected. #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15603 #### Testing - Added `TestUnmarshalJSONLogsRecursionLimit`: shallow nesting still succeeds; nesting past the limit now returns an error rather than being accepted (previously it was accepted, and at larger depths crashed the process with `fatal error: stack overflow`). - Full `pdata` module `go test ./...` passes; `golangci-lint` clean on the changed packages. - Regenerated code is guard-only (each generated `UnmarshalJSON` gains the same 4-line entry check) and `make genpdata` is idempotent. #### Documentation No user-facing documentation changes; a `.chloggen` entry (`bug_fix`, `pkg/pdata`) is included. #### Authorship - [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.

signals.title: [pkg/pdata] avoid allocations in WriteInt64 and WriteUint64
signals.text: <!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue. Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.--> #### Description Replace strconv.FormatInt/FormatUint (which allocate a new string each call) with strconv.AppendInt/AppendUint writing into a stack-allocated [22]byte buffer. The quoted decimal string is then written directly to the jsoniter stream via Write, bypassing any string conversion. Inspired by the same technique used in float64AsString that also uses a scratch buffer. signals.title: [pkg/exporterhelper] Keep the in-flight requests in the persistent queue when they fail during the shutdown
signals.text: <!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue. Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.--> #### Description The requests that failed while the collector was shutting down were deleted from the persistent queue instead of being redelivered after a restart. Only the retry sender reported such failures as shutdown errors, and only when a backoff wait was interrupted, so exporters that don't enable `retry_on_failure` always lost the requests that were in flight when the destination was unavailable. signals.title: fix(memorylimiter): report health status only on state changes
signals.text: #### Description The `memory_limiter` processor currently reports a `StatusOK` event on every memory check while memory usage remains below the soft limit. Since `CheckMemLimits()` runs periodically, this can generate repeated health status events even when the component remains in the same healthy state. This changes the recovery path so that: - `StatusRecoverableError` is reported when the memory limiter enters the refusing state. - `StatusOK` is reported when the memory limiter recovers from the refusing state - no status event is reported while the component remains in the same state. <!-- Issue number if applicable --> #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15751 <!--Describe what testing was performed and which tests were added.--> #### Testing The above changes were tested with `go test ./internal/memorylimiter`. <!--Describe the documentation added.--> #### Documentation <!--Authorship attestation. signals.title: [chore][sharedcomponent] Fix lifecycle status duplication and start-error propagation
signals.text: <!--Ex. Fixing a bug - Describe the bug and how this fixes the issue. Ex. Adding a feature - Explain what this achieves.--> #### Description The `sharedcomponent` wrapper reported its own lifecycle statuses (`Starting`, `Stopping`, etc), which duplicated the lifecycle statuses reported in the component graph. The original reason for this was intentional, but is no longer needed as of #10777 (see https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/issues/14692#issuecomment-5286069213 for details). The duplicates were harmless because the state machine discarded them as invalid self-transitions. This change makes the graph the single source of lifecycle status. `sharedcomponent` reports and routes runtime statuses to each instance. It also returns the start error on every `Start()` call rather than only the first, so a shared component that fails to start reports the failure to every pipeline that shares it. There is no user-observable behavior change: the previous duplicate/omitted events were discarded by the state machine, and the missing start error is currently hidden by the graph aborting on the first start failure. <!-- Issue number if applicable --> #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #14692 <!--Describe what testing was performed and which tests were added.--> #### Testing - Units / manual <!--Authorship attestation. signal.title: [pdata/pprofile] Speed up dictionary merging with an indexed dedup
signal.text: #### Description Hi! In #15084 the cost of merging the profiles dictionary came up (and @dmathieu mentioned [improvement points would be welcome](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-collector/issues/15084#issuecomment-4222053064)), so I took a look at the merge path. The cost is in `Profiles.MergeTo` → `switchDictionary`: every `Set*` does a linear `.Equal` scan of the destination table, once per source entry, which makes a merge quadratic in dictionary size. This PR adds an internal per-merge index (`mergeIndex`) — one lookup structure per table, seeded once from the destination — to replace those scans. The string table uses a `map[string]int32`; the other tables use a hash bucket where the existing `.Equal` is still the arbiter (the hash only narrows candidates), so dedup semantics are unchanged. The public `Set*` API is untouched — only the unexported `switchDictionary` methods change. Output is byte-identical to before (lowest-index-wins preserved), covered by a differential test, a forced hash-collision test, and an end-to-end marshal→merge→unmarshal round-trip. Attribute entries are hashed by the content of their value, not just its type, so a table dominated by one hot key (`thread.name`, `k8s.pod.name`) still spreads across buckets. The value hash has to agree with `pcommon.Value.Equal` or equal values would land in different buckets and append a duplicate where the linear scan deduped: `-0.0` is normalized to `+0.0` (`Equal` compares doubles with `==`), and maps are combined order-independently (`Map.Equal` matches by key, and Go's map iteration order is randomized). **Benchmarks.** `BenchmarkDictionaryMerge` merges a batch of K profiles into one destination. I don't know the real-world distribution of how much profiles in a batch share dictionary symbols, so I swept it: `overlap` is the fraction of a profile's dictionary already present in the destination (0% = fully disjoint, the worst case; 100% = identical profiles). benchstat, n=10, `main` → this PR (AMD Ryzen 7 255, linux/amd64), 20-profile batch: | case | main | this PR | Δ time | |---|---|---|---| | overlap=0% (disjoint) | 65.69 s | 124.0 ms | −99.81% | | overlap=50% | 3.405 s | 78.5 ms | −97.69% | | overlap=90% | 2.738 s | 48.7 ms | −98.22% | | overlap=99% | 3.140 s | 42.0 ms | −98.66% | | batch=5 | 672.9 ms | 11.7 ms | −98.26% | | batch=20 | 2.741 s | 49.3 ms | −98.20% | | batch=50 | 7.100 s | 137.0 ms | −98.07% | | size=0.5x | 709.6 ms | 25.0 ms | −96.48% | | size=1x | 2.741 s | 50.2 ms | −98.17% | | size=2x | 11.12 s | 96.5 ms | −99.13% | | **geomean** | **3.746 s** | **53.5 ms** | **−98.57%** | `BenchmarkDictionaryMergeHotKey` isolates the attribute table under a single hot key carrying many distinct values — the shape that stays quadratic if attribute values are hashed by type rather than content. 10-profile batch: | case | main | this PR | Δ time | |---|---|---|---| | attrs=500 | 8.99 ms | 632 µs | −92.97% | | attrs=2000 | 139.2 ms | 4.18 ms | −97.00% | | attrs=8000 | 2.344 s | 17.0 ms | −99.27% | | **geomean** | **143.1 ms** | **3.56 ms** | **−97.52%** | All differences p=0.000 at n=10. Scaling with dictionary size goes from quadratic to ~linear. Reproduce: `go test ./pdata/pprofile/ -bench BenchmarkDictionaryMerge -benchmem` on this branch vs `main`. Tradeoff: the index trades transient memory for CPU, and the trade is not small in absolute terms. Geomean `B/op` goes up +948% on the sweep (+441% allocs/op) and +947% on the hot-key benchmark (+384%). Since a percentage hides the number worth budgeting for, the peaks: 12.66 MiB → 100.9 MiB per merge at `overlap=0%`, and 3.48 MiB → 68.8 MiB at `batch=50`. The index is rebuilt per `MergeTo`, so it is short-lived garbage freed when the merge returns — but it is a real peak, not an average. If the extra allocation or GC pressure is a concern, the per-merge rebuild can be removed entirely with a destination-resident index or a once-per-flush batch-merge entry point — I kept this PR to the merge path only to stay tightly scoped, and can follow up with that if you'd prefer. #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15544. Related to #15084 (the perf half; the data-corruption half was fixed in #15134). #### Testing New differential + hash-collision tests (`dictionary_merge_index_test.go`) covering every table, including a same-key/distinct-value case for attributes with a bucket-spread assertion; tests that the value hash agrees with `Equal` on `-0.0` and on map ordering; a zero-allocation guard on the value hash; table-overflow guard coverage; and an end-to-end round-trip (`profiles_merge_test.go`). Each new guard was verified to fail without the corresponding fix. `go test ./pdata/pprofile/...` (including `-race`) and `go vet ./pdata/pprofile/` pass, as do the `pdata`, root, `exporter/exporterhelper` and `scraper/scraperhelper` module suites. #### Documentation Changelog entry under `.chloggen/`. #### Authorship - [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.

signal.title: Add recursion depth limit to JSON unmarshalling
signal.text: #### Description The proto unmarshal path bounds recursion depth to guard against stack exhaustion from deeply nested payloads, but the JSON path had no equivalent limit. An `AnyValue` whose value is an `arrayValue`/`kvlistValue` of `AnyValue`s, nested deeply enough, recurses through the generated `UnmarshalJSON` methods until the goroutine stack overflows — a fatal, unrecoverable crash (`recover()` cannot catch it), not just a failed request. It's reachable through the public `JSONUnmarshaler` from any component that decodes untrusted OTLP/JSON without a request-size cap. This tracks nesting depth on the JSON `Iterator` (`EnterRecursive`/`ExitRecursive`, with a limit of 100) and injects the guard at the top of every generated `UnmarshalJSON` via the pdatagen template, so over-limit nesting returns an error instead of overflowing the stack. This mirrors the proto side (#15597). The limit sits well beyond any realistic telemetry nesting — the effective budget is ~47 nested `arrayValue`/`kvlistValue` levels, matching the proto path — so well-formed payloads are unaffected. #### Link to tracking issue Fixes #15603 #### Testing - Added `TestUnmarshalJSONLogsRecursionLimit`: shallow nesting still succeeds; nesting past the limit now returns an error rather than being accepted (previously it was accepted, and at larger depths crashed the process with `fatal error: stack overflow`). - Full `pdata` module `go test ./...` passes; `golangci-lint` clean on the changed packages. - Regenerated code is guard-only (each generated `UnmarshalJSON` gains the same 4-line entry check) and `make genpdata` is idempotent. #### Documentation No user-facing documentation changes; a `.chloggen` entry (`bug_fix`, `pkg/pdata`) is included. #### Authorship - [x] I, a human, wrote this pull request description myself.

The main reason for this release is compatibility with the new lychee `0.24.x` release artifacts. Starting with lychee `v0.24.0`, the archive layout changed, and the `lychee` binary may now be packaged inside a subdirectory. `lychee-action` now detects that layout automatically, so users can upgrade without changing their workflows. If you use: ```yaml uses: lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2 ``` you will get the new version once the floating `v2` tag has been updated. If you pin exact versions, update to: ```yaml uses: lycheeverse/lychee-action@v2.9.0 ``` #### What’s new from lychee `v0.24.x` ##### Better diagnostics lychee now reports line and column numbers for detected links. This makes broken link reports easier to act on, especially in larger documentation sites or generated reports. ##### Text fragment checking lychee can now check URL text fragments, such as links containing `#:~:text=...`. This helps catch links that point to a valid page but no longer points to the intended highlighted text. ##### Sitemap support lychee can now read `sitemap.xml` inputs. This is useful for checking published websites or generated documentation sites where the sitemap is the easiest source of URLs to validate. ##### JUnit output lychee now supports JUnit output. This makes it easier to integrate link checking results with CI systems and test reporting tools that understand JUnit XML. ##### Redirect and remap visibility lychee can now show redirects and remaps more clearly. This helps explain why a URL was checked as a different final URL and makes debugging link-checking behavior easier. ##### Multiple config files lychee now supports multiple configuration files and expanded config handling. This is useful for repositories that split documentation, website, or package-specific link-checking settings. ##### Timeout handling lychee can now accept timeouts explicitly. This gives users more control over how strict their link checks should be for flaky or slow endpoints. #### Fixes and reliability improvements ##### Fixed lychee `0.24.x` archive compatibility `lychee-action` now handles the new lychee release archive layout by detecting whether the `lychee` binary is inside a subdirectory. This fixes compatibility with lychee `0.24.x`. ##### More stable installation path The action now installs lychee into `$RUNNER_TEMP/lychee/bin` instead of `$HOME`. This avoids failures on runners where `$HOME` differs between composite action steps. In those environments, the action could add one directory to `PATH` but install the binary somewhere else, causing `lychee: command not found`. ##### Safer automatic lychee version updates The workflow that checks for new lychee releases now guards against `null` release versions before creating update PRs.
